title: Design Principles (DRY, KISS, YAGNI...)
summary: The practical heuristics beyond SOLID — small rules of thumb that keep everyday code simple, honest, and easy to change.

blocks.markdown:
**Design principles** are the everyday heuristics that guide decisions [solid-principles](solid-principles) doesn't cover — smaller in scope but used far more often.

- They're rules of thumb, not laws — apply with judgment.
- Most exist to fight one thing: **unnecessary complexity**.
- Several pull in different directions, so knowing when they conflict matters as much as knowing them.

blocks.subTitle: Don't Repeat Yourself
blocks.markdown:
**DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)**: every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the system.

- Why: duplicated logic drifts — fix a bug in one copy, forget the other three.
- Pitfall: DRY is about **knowledge**, not text. Two functions that look similar but change for different reasons should stay separate — merging them creates false coupling.

blocks.subTitle: Keep It Simple, Stupid
blocks.markdown:
**KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid)**: prefer the simplest design that solves the problem.

- Why: simple code is easier to read, test, and debug — cleverness is a cost paid by every future reader.
- Pitfall: don't confuse "simple" with "fewest lines." A one-liner regex nobody can parse is not simpler than five clear lines.

blocks.subTitle: You Aren't Gonna Need It
blocks.markdown:
**YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)**: don't build functionality until it's actually needed.

- Why: speculative features cost time now and maintenance forever, and most guesses about "future needs" turn out wrong.
- Pitfall: adding a config flag, plugin hook, or abstract base class for a use case nobody has asked for yet.

blocks.subTitle: DRY vs KISS vs YAGNI
blocks.markdown:
These three can pull against each other — none wins automatically.

- **DRY vs KISS**: chasing zero duplication can produce a tangle of generic helpers and indirection that's harder to follow than three simple copies.
- **DRY vs YAGNI**: extracting a shared abstraction for code that *might* repeat later is speculative work — wait for a third real use ("rule of three") before generalizing.
- Rule of thumb: a little duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

Prefer building behavior by **combining small objects** over extending a base class.

| | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Coupling | Tight to parent | Loose, via interface |
| Flexibility | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| Risk | Fragile base class | Extra indirection |

Why: deep [inheritance](inheritance) trees break when the base class changes. A `Duck` that composes a `FlyBehavior` can swap it; a `Duck extends Bird` is stuck with whatever `Bird` does.

blocks.subTitle: Talk only to close friends
blocks.markdown:
**Law of Demeter**: an object should only call methods on itself, its own fields, its parameters, or objects it creates — not on objects it got back from another call.

- Why: chains like `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()` couple you to the whole object graph; any link changing breaks you.
- Fix: ask the immediate collaborator to do the work — `order.getCityOfDelivery()` — and let it delegate internally.

**Separation of Concerns**: split a system so each part addresses one distinct concern (data access, business rules, presentation) with minimal overlap.

- Why: a change to how data is displayed shouldn't risk breaking how it's validated or stored.
- Pitfall: a controller that also runs SQL and formats HTML has zero separation — three concerns, one file. Related to [coupling-cohesion](coupling-cohesion).

blocks.subTitle: Not an implementation
blocks.markdown:
**Program to an interface, not an implementation**: depend on what an object does, not on its concrete class.

- Why: code that holds a `PaymentMethod` [interfaces-vs-abstract-classes](interfaces-vs-abstract-classes) can accept `CreditCard` or `Wallet` without changes; code that holds a `CreditCard` directly cannot.
- Pitfall: declaring a variable as `ArrayList` instead of `List` locks you to that one implementation for no reason.

**Encapsulate what varies**: identify the part of your code likely to change, and wall it off behind a stable boundary.

- Why: isolating the volatile piece means change stays local instead of rippling through every caller.
- Example: a `TaxCalculator` interface hides per-country tax rules; adding a new country never touches checkout code.

**Single Source of Truth (SSOT)**: every fact should be owned and stored in exactly one place; everywhere else reads or derives from it.

- Why: two places holding the "same" value (a cached total and a recomputed total) will eventually disagree.
- Pitfall: storing a derived field (like `fullName`) alongside its source (`firstName`, `lastName`) instead of computing it on read.

Common ways these principles get misapplied:

- **Over-engineering in the name of DRY or YAGNI-proofing** — building a plugin framework for one caller.
- **Treating Law of Demeter as absolute** — fluent builders (`.setX().setY()`) are chained calls on the *same* object, not a violation.
- **Composition everywhere** — sometimes an "is-a" relationship is genuine and inheritance is the honest model.

blocks.subTitle: DRY, KISS, YAGNI in one breath
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain DRY, KISS, and YAGNI.**

**DRY** — one source of truth for each piece of knowledge, no duplicated logic. **KISS** — pick the simplest design that works; avoid needless cleverness. **YAGNI** — don't build for a future need you're only guessing at.

All three fight the same enemy: complexity that isn't earning its keep.

blocks.subTitle: Why composition over inheritance
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why favor composition over inheritance?**

Inheritance locks a subclass to its parent's implementation at compile time — change the base, and every subclass may break (the fragile base class problem). Composition wires behavior through interfaces at runtime, so pieces can be swapped or tested in isolation. Inheritance still fits genuine "is-a" hierarchies; composition fits "has-a" and "can-do" relationships.

blocks.subTitle: Law of Demeter
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the Law of Demeter and why does it matter?**

It says talk only to your immediate collaborators — not to objects you reach through them. Chains like `a.getB().getC().getD()` hard-wire you to the internal structure of `B` and `C`; if either changes shape, your code breaks even though you never touch them directly.

blocks.subTitle: Can these principles conflict?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Can these principles conflict with each other? Give an example.**

Yes. DRY pushes you to extract shared code; KISS and YAGNI push back if that extraction adds a layer of indirection for a case that may never recur. The practical resolution: tolerate small duplication until a third real usage appears ("rule of three"), then extract — don't generalize on the first repeat.

blocks.subTitle: Program to an interface
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does "program to an interface, not an implementation" buy you?**

Callers depend on behavior (a contract) instead of a concrete class, so you can swap implementations — a real database for an in-memory fake in tests, or one payment provider for another — without touching calling code.

blocks.subTitle: Single Source of Truth
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What problem does "Single Source of Truth" solve?**

It stops the same fact from being stored twice and drifting out of sync — like a cached order total that stops matching its line items after an edit. Every other copy should be a read or a computed view of the one owner, never an independent store.
